name: Symbolic Systems (BS)

rules.desc:
The Symbolic Systems major requires the completion of:

• Core curriculum — a standard set of foundations, breadth requirements, and experiential requirements that all students in the program must complete

• Subplan — an approved concentration and depth in a particular specialization (subplan) chosen by the student; courses of at least three units each that fulfill the requirements for one of the subplan areas below.
Students must submit a course plan to the student services officer for Symbolic Systems at least two quarters before the planned graduation date, listing courses taken or that will be completed to fulfill the course requirements for the major.
Students must obtain approval for courses not listed as approved for a major requirement.
rules.name: Course plan submitted to Symbolic Systems

rules.desc: Core requirements are typically completed earlier than a student’s concentration, but the only requirements that impose explicit restrictions on when a course can be completed during a student’s undergraduate career are the gateway and capstone requirements.

rules.name: Preparations:
rules.desc: These courses should be completed early in the major.

children.name: Calculus and Linear Algebra
children.notes:
• The Symbolic Systems Program recommends MATH rather than CME or ENGR courses as preferred ways for most students to learn multivariate calculus and linear algebra, because of their more extensive coverage of linear algebra methods used in many higher level courses which are options for the major.

• 6 units replacing MATH 19 and 20, or 10 units replacing MATH 19, 20, and 21, earned through Advanced Placement or other international exams can be applied towards the total required 8 units of Single Variable Calculus ( Units cannot be counted for both AP/exam credit and the courses that the credit replaces.)

children.name: Introduction to Multivariate Calculus and Linear Algebra
Single Variable Calculus or other courses in multivariate calculus, linear algebra, and discrete methods.
children.notes: In most cases, a student's first 4 to 10 units toward the Calculus and Linear Algebra requirement will consist of units in the Single Variable Calculus Math 19, 20 and 21 series. A student for whom the Mathematics Placement Diagnostic recommends placement beyond the level for which they have unit credit may take courses contained in this list beyond MATH 51 or CME 100 in Multivariate and Linear Algebra.

rules.name: Advanced Small Seminar Requirement
rules.desc:
One approved course from one of the lists below that (a) builds on the Core Preparations and Breadth Requirements, (b) is small – 20 students or fewer, and (c) is an interactive, discussion-based seminar. May be double-counted for an applicable Concentration (Subplan) requirement, but not for a Core requirement.
Students are encouraged to take an ASSR course within their Concentration, but any approved ASSR course may be taken to fulfill the Core Advanced Small Seminar Requirement.

rules.name: Breadth Requirements Overview
rules.desc:
One three-quarters training sequence in each of the four methodological areas below, plus a Cross-Area Requirement.
Four Methodological Areas:

• Philosophical Analysis

• Formal Methods

• Computational Methods

• Empirical Cognitive Science

rules.name: 1. Philosophical Analysis
rules.desc: Courses that focus on critical, deep questioning, careful reasoning, introspection, and argumentation, and the meaning of intuitions, scenarios, and evidence.

children.name: Introductory Philosophy
children.desc: An introductory course in the Philosophy Department taught by a Philosophy Department faculty member. One of the following:
children.notes: • Any course of three units or more listed with a PHIL course number (except PHIL 99/SYMSYS 1)

children.name: Advanced Philosophy
children.desc: An advanced undergraduate Philosophy course that lists PHIL 80 as a prerequisite. Note that the Writing in the Major requirement (Phil 80) must be completed prior to completing this Advanced Philosophy requirement.

rules.name: 2. Formal Methods
rules.desc:
Courses that focus on rigorous definitions, axioms, theorems, and proofs and their use in developing mathematical theories and meta-theories.
Choose one course from each of the following categories:

• Formal Logic

• Theory of Computation

• Probability Theory & Statistics

children.name: Formal Logic
children.notes: PHIL 151 carries a prerequisite of PHIL 150.

children.name: Probability Theory & Statistics
children.desc: A course that covers the theory of probability and is grounded in multivariable calculus.

rules.name: 3. Computational Methods
rules.desc:
Courses focusing on software design, data structures, algorithms, development, applications, evaluation, and simulation.
Choose one course from each of the following categories:

• Programming I

• Programming II

• A post-CS 106B Course - covering one or more broad computational methods with a programming component

children.name: Programming I
children.notes: Or equivalent preparation, as evidenced by successful completion of CS 106B.

children.name: Post-CS 106B Course
children.desc: A course covering one or more broad computational methods with a programming component.

rules.name: 4. Empirical Cognitive Science
rules.desc:
Courses that focus on questions, hypotheses, models, predictions, and explanations derived from or testable in neural and behavioral data.
Complete one course from each of the following categories:

• Overview of Psychology

• An Introductory Course in Cognition, Language, & Neuroscience

• Linguistic Theory

children.name: Introductory Course in Cognition, Language, & Neuroscience

rules.name: Cross-Area Requirement
rules.desc:
A non-introductory course, which has as a prerequisite of at least one Core course (or equivalent), which combines methods and subject matter from at least two Breadth areas.
Only one course must be chosen to fulfill the requirement. The following categories are for guidance only:

• Suggested Courses for Most Students

• Philosophical Analysis & Formal Methods

• Philosophical Analysis & Computational Methods

• Philosophical Analysis & Empirical Cognitive Science

• Formal Methods & Computational Methods

• Formal Methods & Empirical Cognitive Science

• Computational Methods & Empirical Cognitive Science

rules.name: Capstone Overview
rules.desc:
An experiential requirement consisting of the following components, chosen in consultation with, and approved by, a student’s Concentration (Subplan) Adviser (3 or more units each).
To obtain approval for your Capstone plan, submit the Capstone Approval Form. This form must be submitted in addition to your SYMSYS Course Plan. Additionally, your Capstone plan is subject to final approval by the Symbolic Systems Program office and must be approved by the end of the first week of Winter Quarter, Junior Year (8th quarter) or a hold will be placed on Spring quarter registration.

rules.name: Presentation Requirement (not a course requirement, check-off only)
rules.desc:
A public presentation of the student’s work at one of the following annual events:

• Symbolic Systems Autumn Poster Fair for Summer Interns and Capstone Projects,

• Symbolic Systems Spring Graduation Fair for Capstone and Master’s Projects, or

• Symbolic Systems Senior Honors Forum at the end of spring quarter

rules.name: Honors thesis
rules.desc:
Seniors in SSP may apply for admission to the Symbolic Systems honors program before their final year of study begins. Students who are accepted into the honors program can graduate with honors by completing an honors thesis under the supervision of a faculty member. Course credit for the honors project may be obtained by registering for SYMSYS 190 Senior Honors Tutorial any quarter while a student works on an honors project. SYMSYS 191 Senior Honors Seminar is recommended for honors students during their senior year. Contact SSP or visit the program’s website for more information on the honors program, including deadlines and policies.
In order to be considered for Honors, students must:

• Be a junior or senior

• Be in good academic standing, with at least a 3.0 GPA

• Submit an acceptable honors project proposal
For more information, visit the Symbolic Systems website.

rules.name: Individually Designed Concentrations (IDCs)
rules.desc:
(Concentrations referred to as Subplans within Bulletin and Degree Guide)
Individually Designed Concentrations (IDCs) consist of five courses in a coherent subject area related to symbolic systems. This relationship may be established through inclusion in an IDC of two or more courses that connect the proposed concentration to the core, i.e., courses that (a) directly apply disciplines included in the core and (b) are related by topic or methodology to the other courses in the proposed concentration.
Course selection is to be made in consultation with the student’s advisor and is subject to approval by the advisor, the Associate Director, and the Director. For examples of IDCs completed by past SSP students, consult the alumni list and apply the filter “Individually Designed Concentration.”
Approval of an IDC must take place no less than two full quarters before a student plans to graduate, e.g., before the first day of winter quarter of the senior year if a student intends to graduate in June of that year. Failure to obtain approval by the required date will necessitate either completing the requirements for one of the suggested concentrations or delaying graduation to the end of the second full quarter following approval of an IDC.
To get a proposed IDC approved, send an email message to symsys-directors at lists.stanford.edu, cc’d to your prospective concentration advisor, stating that the advisor has approved your proposal and giving a title, one-paragraph description, and course plan for your proposed concentration.

grading: All courses taken to fulfill a major requirement for Symbolic Systems must be passed for three units or more, with either a letter grade (C- or better for core courses, and a D- or above for concentration courses), a no-option pass grade (S or its equivalent in the Graduate School of Business, Stanford Law School, or School of Medicine, or in an approved transfer credit course from another institution. A CR cannot be used to fulfill a significant requirement for Symbolic Systems). Students who have already completed a required course with a CR grade may file a Replacement Petition to take a course in the same subject area at the same or a higher level to avoid having to retake the course.
policies:
Unless otherwise stated, each course counted for the major must be taken for three units or more. Taking a course for three units is sufficient unless the requirement specifically states otherwise.
Each course taken for the major may be counted toward only one required course in either the Core or Subplan (not both), except in cases where double-counting is explicitly allowed.
Students in a Dual Degree Program, students taking a minor, or students in a Coterminal Program, may not double-count courses towards different degree programs or minors unless a course is an Introductory Skill Requirement for both majors.
The program is open to requests to approve courses not listed as options to fulfill major requirements. Consult the student services office for details of this process.
transferPolicy:
An external course taken at another college or university can be proposed to fulfill a requirement as a replacement for an approved Stanford course. Note especially the following for this type of petition:

• Evidence must be provided that the course is substantially similar in content, level, and rigor to one or more Stanford courses that meet the requirement. If available, a link to the course description online and a syllabus can serve as evidence, along with reading material and other assignments. The course prerequisites should be similar to those listed for the Stanford course(s) it is intended to replace.

• The proposed external course must be eligible for three units or more of transfer credit at Stanford, as determined by the Registrar’s Office.

• You can consult the Registrar’s Office Transfer Credit Database and Course Equivalency List to identify courses at other institutions that may be appropriate to replace a Stanford course. The appearance of a pair of courses on the equivalency list does not guarantee that the SymSys Program will accept the transfer course in place of the Stanford course in the pairing, but the equivalency list is a good indication of courses that may be appropriate as replacements.

• The proposed external course must generate a number of Stanford units equivalent to the course(s) being replaced.
For further information on Replacement Petitions, please visit this page: Replacement Petitions | Symbolic Systems Program (stanford.edu)
reviewNotes: You take the Core (the gateway course, calculus and linear algebra, the Advanced Small Seminar, the four breadth areas, the WIM and the capstone) and one subplan's courses, for 70 units. Every course must be taken for at least 3 units and letter graded, or passed with an S where only S/NC is offered; CR does not count. Core courses need a C- or better, subplan courses a D- or better, and a course counts toward one requirement unless double counting is allowed. Your course plan, capstone plan, presentation and honors are checked by hand.
